stimulus.text: "In the name of God, Amen.... Having undertaken for the Glory of God and advancement of the Christian Faith, and the Honor of our King and Country, a Voyage to plant the First Colony in the Northern Parts of Virginia, do by these presents, solemnly and mutually, in the presence of God and one another, covenant and combine ourselves together into a civil body politic, for our better ordering and preservation.... In witness whereof we have hereunder subscribed our names at Cape Cod, the 11th of November.... Anno Domini 1620." — Signed November 11, 1620; text as printed in Mourt's Relation (1622) and Bradford's Of Plymouth Plantation.
stimulus.source_note: Mayflower Compact, signed November 11, 1620; text as printed in Mourt's Relation (1622) and Bradford's Of Plymouth Plantation; public domain.

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim public-domain primary source

books.section: Massachusetts and the New England Colonies

stem: What does the Compact's creation of a “civil body politic” best show about the Plymouth settlers?

options.text: That they rejected all government authority.
options.misconception: The settlers did not reject government; they created one, covenanting together into a civil body politic.

options.text: That they claimed independence from England.
options.misconception: They called themselves loyal subjects of King James; the Compact claims no independence from England.

options.text: That they planned to return to England within a year.
options.misconception: Nothing in the Compact speaks of returning; they covenant to order a colony for the general good.

options.text: That they would govern themselves by laws made together.

rationales.general:
1. Read what they did. They covenanted and combined themselves into a civil body politic.
2. Read what that body would do. Background: the Compact promises just and equal laws, ordinances, and offices for the general good.
3. Ask who makes those laws. They themselves, together — not a governor sent from London.
4. Name the point. Self-government by agreement, made on the spot at Cape Cod.
Remember: the Compact is a government the settlers made themselves — laws by mutual covenant, not by royal order.
rationales.D: The Compact shows the settlers governing themselves by agreement: finding themselves outside any colony's jurisdiction, they covenanted together into a civil body politic. Background: they promised to enact “just and equal Laws, Ordinances, Acts, Constitutions and Offices” for the general good. Background: they still called themselves loyal subjects of King James, so this was self-government within the English world, not independence. They rejected no government and planned no return; they made one.
rationales.A: The settlers did not reject government; they created one, covenanting together into a civil body politic.
rationales.B: They called themselves loyal subjects of King James; the Compact claims no independence from England.
rationales.C: Nothing in the Compact speaks of returning; they covenant to order a colony for the general good.
